crater-counting.title: Crater Counting
crater-counting.info: A way to date a surface you cannot yet touch, from orbit alone. A fresh lava flow starts bare; craters accumulate at a known rate, so their density gives a relative age — calibrated against radiometrically dated Moon rocks. Click craters to tally them.
crater-counting.hint: Click each crater to count it. Denser fields are older.

deep-time.title: Deep Time
deep-time.info: Geology's vast timescale — millions to billions of years, far beyond human intuition. The spiral compresses the recent past and stretches the deep past so all 4.5 Gyr fit in one frame. Travel back and watch the great events flare.

geochronology.title: Geochronology
geochronology.info: The science of putting numerical ages on rocks. No single clock spans all of time — each radiometric method reads only its own window. Drag a target age and watch which clocks can read it and which go blind.

geologic-time-scale.title: Geologic Time Scale
geologic-time-scale.info: The calendar that splits Earth's history into eons, built by marrying relative order from strata with absolute radiometric ages. Bar heights are true durations — all of complex visible life is the thin sliver at the top. Hover an eon to read it.
geologic-time-scale.hint: Hover a band to read its eon.
geologic-time-scale.phanerozoicDesc: The eon of visible life — from the Cambrian explosion through to today. All of animals, plants, and us fit here.
geologic-time-scale.proterozoicDesc: The long age of microbes and rising oxygen, ending as the first complex life stirred.
geologic-time-scale.archeanDesc: The world of the earliest life — single cells in a sky with no free oxygen.
geologic-time-scale.hadeanDesc: The infernal beginning: a molten crust, relentless impacts, and the first zircons.

half-life.title: Half-Life
half-life.info: The time for half the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay. Each atom decays by pure chance, yet the population halves so regularly the curve can be run backward to read an age. Press play — the lattice is 100 atoms; the dashed line is the ideal law.
half-life.curveAria: Decay curve of remaining parent atoms versus elapsed half-lives

isochron.title: Isochron
isochron.info: A dating method that defeats the question 'how much daughter was there to start?'. Several minerals from one melt begin on a flat line; as decay proceeds the line pivots and steepens. Its slope gives the age, its intercept recovers the initial ratio — no assumption needed.

radiocarbon-dating.title: Radiocarbon Dating
radiocarbon-dating.info: Carbon-14 dating is superb for the recent past — wood, bone, charcoal. But its half-life is only ~5,730 years, so past ~50,000 years there is essentially no parent left to measure. Drag the measured fraction and read the age — until the sample falls off the wall.

radiometric-dating.title: Radiometric Dating
radiometric-dating.info: A rock's age from the ratio of leftover radioactive 'parent' atoms to the 'daughter' atoms they decay into. The decay rate is a constant no heat, pressure, or chemistry can change — a clock that cannot be bribed. Watch parents (cyan) flip to daughters (magenta).
radiometric-dating.hint: The daughter/parent ratio climbs the calibration curve.
radiometric-dating.calAria: Calibration curve of daughter-to-parent ratio versus age

uniformitarianism.title: Uniformitarianism
uniformitarianism.info: The present is the key to the past: the slow processes at work today are the same ones that built the past, at broadly the same rates. A millimetre of silt per year seems like nothing — yet run it across deep time and it stacks into kilometres of rock.

uranium-lead-dating.title: Uranium–Lead Dating
uranium-lead-dating.info: The gold-standard clock for deep time, hosted in zircon. Two uranium isotopes decay to two lead isotopes at two very different rates — two independent clocks in one grain. Plotted together they trace 'concordia'; an undisturbed grain rides exactly on it.
uranium-lead-dating.crystalAria: Zircon crystal cross-section accumulating lead as decay proceeds
uranium-lead-dating.concordiaAria: Concordia diagram with the grain riding on the curve

zircon.title: Zircon
zircon.info: A tiny, nearly indestructible crystal — the ideal host for uranium-lead dating. It locks in uranium but shuts out lead, so its clock starts clean. Under cathodoluminescence its growth zones glow: on Pandora, the bright core dates the moon's birth and the paler rim the ancient impact. Click a zone; drag to rotate.
zircon.dragHint: Drag to rotate · click a zone
zircon.coreNote: The core: Pandora's first crust, crystallized near the system's birth ~4.5 Gyr ago.
zircon.innerNote: An early growth zone, added as the young crust cooled.
zircon.bandNote: A concentric band recording steady growth over deep time.
zircon.rimNote: The paler rim: regrown around the Mars-sized impact that forged unobtanium — a younger date in the same grain.
